patient.chief_complaint: Daughter noticed increased confusion and word-finding difficulty for 3 days
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. D. is a 57-year-old woman with HCV-related cirrhosis who achieved sustained virologic response 2 months ago with direct-acting antiviral therapy, presenting at her daughter's insistence with a 3-day history of increasing confusion, word-finding difficulty, and personality change. The daughter noted her mother had been more forgetful, had missed two medication doses this week, was having difficulty balancing her checkbook (which she typically manages perfectly), and had been sleeping 12-14 hours per day. The patient herself minimized symptoms. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. She denied hematemesis or melena. She denied changes in her methadone dose or missed doses. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal discomfort over the prior week and constipation. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago. She had been started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) one week ago by her primary care physician for a urinary tract infection — this medication is generally avoided in cirrhosis as it can precipitate HE. The precipitant in this case required careful consideration: (1) constipation, (2) TMP-SMX (antibiotic that alters gut flora reducing lactulose efficacy), and (3) mildly elevated TSH suggesting undertreated hypothyroidism — all contributing to moderate HE in a patient with otherwise compensated cirrhosis.

output.query: Hepatic encephalopathy after HCV SVR cirrhosis — does SVR eliminate HE risk

results.title: Risk of hepatic decompensation after SVR in HCV-related cirrhosis
results.summary: SVR significantly reduces but does not eliminate risk of hepatic decompensation including HE in patients with established cirrhosis. Cirrhosis may partially reverse (Child-Pugh improvement) but portal hypertension may persist. HE risk remains, particularly with additional precipitants (constipation, infection, drugs). Lifelong surveillance and HE prophylaxis may be needed in cirrhotic patients even after SVR.

output.summary: SVR significantly reduces but does not eliminate the risk of hepatic decompensation including hepatic encephalopathy in patients with established cirrhosis. Published cohort data indicate that HE events continue to occur post-SVR, particularly when additional precipitants are present. Clinical correlation recommended.

Increase levothyroxine dose — TSH 8.4; undertreated hypothyroidism contributing

critical_actions: Identify ALL precipitants — constipation, TMP-SMX, and hypothyroidism are all contributing; address each
Discontinue TMP-SMX — in cirrhosis, antibiotics that alter gut flora (especially TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolones) can precipitate HE; replace with nitrofurantoin if UTI confirmed
TSH elevation requires treatment — hypothyroid encephalopathy can both mimic and worsen HE; levothyroxine dose increase appropriate
SVR does not eliminate HE risk in established cirrhosis — patient requires continued HE prophylaxis
contraindicated_actions: TMP-SMX in cirrhosis — precipitates HE via gut flora disruption; use nitrofurantoin for UTI
Opioid dose escalation without clear indication
key_reasoning_points: TMP-SMX is frequently prescribed without recognizing HE precipitation risk in cirrhosis — the antibiotic disrupts the gut microbiome that lactulose and rifaximin target
Undertreated hypothyroidism can both contribute to and mimic HE — TSH should be checked in any confusion workup, especially in women over 50
Methadone in opioid use disorder maintenance is NOT the cause of encephalopathy when levels are therapeutic — methadone should NOT be discontinued without addiction medicine involvement
SVR does not reverse established cirrhosis — HCV-cured cirrhotic patients remain at risk for HE and require ongoing hepatology care
